question: Can every decision be modeled as two complementary Bayesian processes, and does that model justify fixed golden-ratio-derived values for SGD momentum and learning rate?

key_findings.claim: The paper postulates a dual Bayesian decision process in which each side has complementary knowledge and uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Motivated by sender/receiver interpretations of the Rubin vase, the framework factorizes a binary decision into input encoding and input-output relation decisions, then introduces logarithm bases as control parameters and fixed points.

key_findings.claim: Golden-ratio algebra is used to propose momentum 0.874 and learning rate 0.016.
key_findings.evidence: Starting from p=(sqrt(5)-1)/2, the author maps equal inner-Bayes multiplicands to alpha=sqrt(2)p≈0.874, then takes the squared complement eta=(1-alpha)^2≈0.016. The mapping from the abstract Bayesian factors to successive SGD gradients is asserted rather than derived from an optimization objective or loss geometry.

key_findings.claim: A two-dimensional MNIST grid search places the proposed pair among the best tested settings.
key_findings.evidence: A roughly 200k-parameter CNN is trained for 30 epochs with 10-fold cross-validation on full and 50% MNIST. The 6x10 grid explicitly includes 0.016 and 0.874; on full data it ties other pairs for first, and on half data it is reported best.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2, grid and full-data result

key_findings.claim: The empirical evidence is too narrow to establish universal or even broadly robust optimizer constants.
key_findings.evidence: Only one CNN/dataset and a hand-selected coarse grid are tested, at about 270 total GPU-hours. There are no modern adaptive or scheduled optimizer baselines, no statistical comparisons among tied settings, and no transfer across architectures, batch sizes or loss curvature.

anchors.section: Discussion and acknowledged need for more experiments

method.core_idea: Represent decision-making as two interdependent Bayesian processes and map fixed points of the resulting equations to fixed SGD hyperparameters.
method.mechanism: Construct inner and outer Bayes equations, parameterize them with logarithm bases, identify golden-ratio fixed points, interpret current and previous gradient terms as dual processes, and evaluate the derived momentum/learning-rate pair in a grid search.
assumptions: Every relevant decision decomposes into exactly two complementary Bayesian decisions.
The algebraic factors in the Bayes construction correspond to SGD gradient and momentum terms.
A universal fixed pair can be meaningful despite task-, scale- and curvature-dependent optimization dynamics.
MNIST grid-search performance can corroborate the theoretical mapping.

techniques.role: Postulates complementary decision processes with asymmetric information.
Maps the fixed point to momentum and learning-rate constants.
Tests 60 fixed hyperparameter pairs on MNIST.

evaluations.setting: Full MNIST with a two-convolution-layer CNN, batch size 64, 30 epochs and 10-fold cross-validation.
evaluations.metric: Classification accuracy over a 6-by-10 learning-rate/momentum grid.
evaluations.result: The proposed (0.016, 0.874) pair ties for the best reported accuracy; several other pairs are equally best.
evaluations.baseline: Other hand-selected fixed pairs, not adaptive optimizers or tuned schedules.

evaluations.metric: Classification accuracy on the same grid.
evaluations.result: The proposed pair is reported as best in the heatmap.
evaluations.baseline: The same coarse set of 59 alternative fixed pairs.

evaluations.result: Sixty combinations on full and half data consume approximately 270 GPU-hours and roughly 1 GB per run.
evaluations.baseline: No efficiency comparison against principled hyperparameter search or adaptive methods.

limitations: The dual-process premise and its correspondence to SGD terms are postulates, not consequences of Bayes decision theory.
The golden ratio follows from the constructed quadratic but does not establish optimizer optimality.
One small vision dataset and one CNN cannot support a universal hyperparameter claim.
The grid includes the exact proposed values and has uneven, coarse spacing; ties and selection effects are not statistically analyzed.
No comparison is made against Adam, adaptive learning rates, schedules, Nesterov momentum or tuned random search.
Learning-rate scale changes with batch size, parameterization, normalization and objective curvature.
The speculative links to brain waves and quantum uncertainty are not empirically tested.
failure_modes: The fixed learning rate diverges or trains slowly when curvature or parameter scale differs from MNIST.
The apparent optimum disappears under a denser or unbiased hyperparameter search.
A learning-rate schedule or adaptive optimizer dominates every fixed pair.
Cross-validation folds are treated as independent evidence despite shared design and hyperparameter selection.
The Bayesian metaphor is mistaken for a mechanistic account of neural optimization.
reusable_insights: A derived optimizer constant should be validated across scale, architecture, batch size, data modality and curvature-controlled synthetic objectives.
Hyperparameter theories need preregistered search spaces and comparisons with equal tuning budgets.
Tied grid-search winners are evidence of a broad plateau, not precise identification of a constant.
Algebraic elegance and optimizer optimality are separate claims requiring separate tests.
open_questions: Can the double-Bayesian premise be formalized as an optimization objective with convergence guarantees?
Does the proposed pair remain Pareto-competitive under schedules and adaptive optimizers at equal compute?
How does the mapping transform under rescaling of loss, batch size or parameterization?
Would preregistered broad benchmarks reproduce the MNIST result?

competitive_landscape.title: The Golden Ratio of Learning and Momentum
competitive_landscape.difference: The earlier paper already derives golden-ratio-related learning and momentum values from an information-theoretic loss; Double-Bayesian Learning reframes and extends that argument through paired Bayesian decisions.

competitive_landscape.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Adam adapts effective step sizes from gradient moments and is evaluated across tasks; the reviewed paper proposes one fixed SGD learning-rate/momentum pair without an adaptive baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Random search motivates unbiased coverage when only some dimensions matter; the reviewed evaluation uses a hand-designed grid centered partly around its theoretically favored values.

competitive_landscape.title: A Large Batch Optimizer Reality Check: Traditional, Generic Optimizers Suffice Across Batch Sizes
competitive_landscape.difference: This work shows that optimizer conclusions can reverse after careful, equal-budget tuning at ImageNet scale; it highlights the validation standard missing from the single-dataset golden-ratio claim.

novelty_assessment: The double-Bayesian construction is an original speculative interpretation, but the optimizer recommendation is not convincingly derived and its empirical support is circularly narrow. A strong follow-up would treat 0.016/0.874 as a falsifiable prior and perform preregistered, equal-budget tests rather than claiming a generally optimal pair.
reviewer_notes: Read all 14 pages, including equations 26-34, stated limitations, the full MNIST setup, heatmaps and 270-GPU-hour accounting. Four direct primary optimization/hyperparameter comparators were checked on 2026-08-23.
